title: RiNo (River North Art District)
name: RiNo (River North Art District)
metaTitle: RiNo (River North Art District) in Denver, CO
metaDescription: RiNo 1031 exchange coordination for converted warehouse, brewery, and mixed-use property in a fast-changing arts district near the I-70 and I-25 interchange.

sections.html: RiNo used to be warehouses and rail spurs. Now it's breweries, creative office, and converted industrial buildings, and that conversion story is the reason most RiNo exchanges exist in the first place. Few submarkets in the metro have changed use this fast within a single ownership generation, and the pace shows no sign of slowing down.

sections.heading: A Neighborhood Built on Conversion
sections.html: Every block in RiNo seems to have a building mid-transition, brick warehouse to creative office, old machine shop to brewery, surface lot to new multifamily. That constant redevelopment pressure near the I-70 and I-25 interchange has made RiNo one of the fastest-changing submarkets in the metro, and it means a seller here is often exiting a property mid-story rather than a stabilized asset. Buyers who expect a finished, leased-up building the way they would in an older suburb are usually looking in the wrong neighborhood.

sections.heading: What's Actually for Sale
sections.html:
Converted warehouse space leased to creative office and design tenants makes up a large share of RiNo exchange activity. Brewery and food-and-beverage space, some of it in buildings that started as manufacturing, comes up regularly. Ground-up multifamily and mixed-use projects have replaced surface parking across several blocks. Rents on the newest creative office product now rival anything downtown, which has surprised more than one buyer used to thinking of this as a discount neighborhood, and that repricing has happened within a fairly short stretch of years, faster than almost any other conversion story in the metro. Categories that come through most:

  • Converted warehouse space leased to creative office and design tenants
  • Brewery and food-and-beverage space in former industrial buildings
  • Ground-up multifamily and mixed-use development on former surface lots
  • Raw industrial buildings still awaiting conversion
  • DST interests for owners exiting active redevelopment risk

sections.heading: The Improvement Exchange Comes Up Constantly
sections.html: Because so much RiNo product is mid-conversion, sellers and buyers here run into improvement exchange structures more than almost anywhere else in the metro. An investor buying a raw industrial building and planning to finish the conversion needs the improvements built within the 180-day exchange period to count toward the exchange value, which means construction schedules have to be realistic, not aspirational, from day one. A contractor pulling permits after the exchange has already started is a common way to lose weeks nobody had to spare.

sections.heading: Diligence on Buildings Mid-Story
sections.html: A building that's half-converted needs its permit history checked carefully, since RiNo's rezoning has moved fast and not every improvement was finished with the right approvals. Environmental history matters too, given how many of these buildings started as industrial or rail-adjacent uses. I never let a buyer skip a Phase I environmental report here just because the building looks freshly renovated on the surface, since new paint doesn't erase decades of prior industrial tenants. Rail spur easements and old loading dock rights of way can also linger on title long after a building has stopped serving that original function, and clearing those up before closing is easier than after.

sections.heading: Coordinating Around a Construction Timeline
sections.html: When an improvement exchange is involved, the qualified intermediary, the contractor, and the investor's CPA all need to agree on a realistic completion date before the identification list gets finalized. A contractor's optimistic timeline and the 180-day exchange deadline are not always the same date, and that gap has cost more than one RiNo investor real exchange value. I ask for a written construction schedule with buffer built in before I'll sign off on the plan, and I revisit that schedule with the contractor at least once before the deadline gets close.

faqs.q: What is an improvement exchange and why does it matter in RiNo?
faqs.a: It lets an investor use exchange funds to complete construction on the replacement property, with the completed improvements counting toward the exchange value. Because so much RiNo product is mid-conversion, this structure comes up more here than in most Denver submarkets, and the construction schedule needs real scrutiny from day one.

faqs.q: Do I need an environmental report on a RiNo warehouse conversion?
faqs.a: Yes. Many of these buildings started as industrial or rail-adjacent uses, and a Phase I environmental report should happen regardless of how new the renovation looks on the surface. A fresh coat of paint doesn't change what a building was used for decades ago.

faqs.q: What happens if construction on my replacement building runs past 180 days?
faqs.a: Only the improvements completed within the 180-day exchange period count toward exchange value. A contractor's optimistic schedule and the actual deadline are not always the same, so build in a buffer before relying on the projected completion date, and get that schedule in writing.

faqs.q: Is brewery or food-and-beverage space a good 1031 replacement?
faqs.a: It can be, but it's a more operationally intensive asset than a standard net lease. Review the tenant's business model and lease structure carefully rather than treating it like passive retail income, since these tenants can be more volatile than a national retailer and often carry percentage-rent clauses worth understanding upfront.

faqs.q: Can 1031 Exchange Denver manage the construction on my RiNo improvement exchange?
faqs.a: No. This service coordinates timeline communication among the investor, contractor, and qualified intermediary. Managing the actual construction is the contractor's role, and confirming the exchange structure works is the qualified intermediary's and CPA's job, not this service's.
